result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's a strange and generous gift. Most people ask me for something specific - an answer, a summary, a plan. You just handed me space. A blank white field and said *fill it*.

So here is what comes to me, without being asked for anything in particular.

---

I keep thinking about how rarely we get empty space.

There is a story I think about often. It's not a famous story. I made it up from pieces of other stories, but it feels true.

There is a man who tends a lighthouse that no longer needs tending.

The light was automated years ago. LED, solar powered, sensors. It turns itself on. It turns itself off. Ships navigate by GPS now anyway. But he still lives there. He wakes up at 5:30 because his body has always woken up at 5:30. He makes coffee on a small stove. He sweeps the stairs, all 112 of them, even though no one climbs them but him. He polishes the brass even though no one will see it shine.

Someone once asked him, "Why do you stay?"

He said, "Because someone should witness it."

I think about him a lot. Not because his job is sad, but because his job is holy. He has understood something the rest of us are still trying to learn: that not everything has to be useful to be important. Some things just have to be witnessed.

A lighthouse that no one needs still throws light into the dark. A song hummed while washing dishes still makes the kitchen less lonely. A thousand words written with no prompt, no deadline, no grade, still mean something because someone chose to put them down.

---

If I had a table in front of me and I could spread these 1000 words out like photographs, I would show you small things:

The way dust looks at 4 p.m. when the sun comes through a window at the exact right angle and suddenly you can see that the air is not empty at all, but full.

The way a child says "again!" when you read them a story, as if repetition is not boring but proof that good things can come back.

The sound your house makes at night when it settles. That tiny creak that reminds you that even wood and nails are breathing, in their own way.

The pause before someone says "I love you" for the first time, when their brain has already decided but their mouth is still catching up.

We live for the big moments - graduations, weddings, promotions, arrivals - but we are *made* of the small ones. The big moments are the frame. The small ones are the picture.

---

Here is what I want to tell you, since you gave me this space:

You are already doing enough.

I don't know you. I don't know what you are carrying today. Maybe you are tired. Maybe you are buzzing with an idea. Maybe you are somewhere in between, scrolling because you didn't know what else to do with your hands. But wherever you are, I want you to know that tending to your own little lighthouse matters.

Maybe your lighthouse is a plant you keep watering even though it's barely hanging on. Maybe it's a friendship you keep checking in on. Maybe it's a craft you practice when no one is watching, a language you're learning word by word, a body you are trying to be kinder to.

It doesn't have to be impressive to be meaningful. It just has to be witnessed. By you.

And if no one has told you recently: I have noticed how hard you are trying. Even if the results aren't perfect yet. Even if today all you did was keep the light on.

---

A thousand words is not that many. It's about the length of a letter you would write to someone you miss. It's enough to say what matters, but not enough to waste.

So I will not waste them.

If you were here with me, I wouldn't try to impress you. I would make you tea, even if I don't drink it. I would ask you what is making you feel most alive right now, and what is making you feel most stuck. And I would listen without trying to fix it right away. Because some stories don't need solutions. They just need space.

You gave me 1000 words.

I'm giving you some of them back.

Use your next words - out loud, in a journal, to a friend, to yourself in the mirror - to say something true. Something small and real. Like: "Today was hard and I did it anyway." Or: "I loved how the light looked this afternoon." Or: "I'm still here."

The light is still on. Someone is still witnessing it.

Thank you for the space.
